1. I notice that this graph includes many overlapping categories, such as democratic men, 34-year-old
women, etc. I guess this data would change if they used more specific categories, rather than general
ones. I find it interesting how the men have a greater number of "not at all serious" and "not very serious"
responses than the women, but also have a greater number of "very serious" responses than the women as
well.

within the subject of free speech, I wonder why they didn't include more specific categories. For one, it
would make sense if they included more intersections, such as Black women, Asian men, etc. I think
including views of minorities who have to regularly censor themselves in fear of retaliation would be
more meaningful and useful data.
3. Personally, I think it is an issue that Americans do not exercise their freedom of speech in everyday
situations in fear of retaliation or harsh criticism, but in the context of them needing to do it for their own
survival. For minorities, censorship is something that many people unfortunately have to do, and have to
code switch and adjust to a eurocentric standard. I think that this is an issue that extends beyond the
simple gender, political view, and age categories, and needs to be acknowledged in a more focused and
relevant context.
4. Free Speech – Does it come at a cost?

Thanks to all of the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  "Majority of Americans Fear Exercising Freedom of Speech" by Joe of Taiwan; “Free Speech May Not Be So Free” by Jania and “Fear Is Taking Our Voices!” by Solomiya, both of Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey; and “Speech Is Free, But the Consequences Aren't.” by Edward, "Fear to Speak on Opinions Through the Eyes of Different Groups" by Lilly and “Do People Think There Is a Cost to "Free" Speech?” by Rory, all three of Winter Garden in Florida.
 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, April 29 to see the Reveal with the free link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who sees her students more mum in class discussions because they are unsure of the reaction of their peers, and Tara Truesdale of Columbia, South Carolina, who enjoys hearing from people who think differently, even if a little tea is spilled.

The first thing that I noticed in this graph was that in general, most people think it is somewhat serious that some Americans do not exercise their freedom of speech due to fear. Within that, Democrats and Americans aged 18-34 are both the highest groups that believe this issue is somewhat serious. Conversely, Democrats have the lowest amount of individuals who think it is very serious. One thing that makes sense to me is that women were one of the highest groups of people who think it is somewhat serious and very serious. I think that this is due to a number of factors. Many women experience sexism & discrimination regularly in their everyday lives, and oftentimes probably hold back on what they really want to say in order to be safe. This is reinforced when you look at the male groups, who have the lowest numbers in both categories, which makes sense since they don't experience the same problems as women. Another thing that I noticed was that more Republicans believe that not exercising their freedom of speech out of fear was considered more serious than Democrats, even though the numbers are opposite for the somewhat serious category.

I wonder what the threshold is for something that is considered "very serious" versus "somewhat serious." Moreover, what are the demographics of race, ethnicity, and where they live? This dramatically affects the results.

This affects me and my community because I deserve to live my life being able to say what I want without criticism.

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows responses to a national poll commissioned by the New York Times about what Americans think about problems we may now have with free speech and cancel culture.   This may have you ask:  How are free of speech and cancel culture related?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, April 29 with moderation on Wednesday, May 4.  The topic – hotter summer temperatures.  Keep noticing and wondering.
